AP® World History Units 2–5: Spread, empires and power, 1200–1900

6 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

Aligned to AP World History: Modern, Unit 2 · 2.5 Cultural Consequences of Connectivity; Unit 3 · 3.2 Empires: Administration; Unit 3 · 3.3 Empires: Belief Systems; Unit 4 · 4.5 Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed; Unit 5 · 5.1 The Enlightenment

Short, curiosity-driven missions (about 20 minutes each) that teachers can assign. Use them alongside AP Classroom practice.

  1. Mission 1Between 1200 and 1450, religions crossed oceans and deserts. Who actually carried them?
  2. Mission 2How did a split inside Western Christianity end up spreading the faith around the world?
  3. Mission 3Emperors, sultans and kings all claimed heaven was on their side. How did they make people believe it?
  4. Mission 4Guru Nanak grew up among Hindus and Muslims. Why do Sikhs say their faith is neither?
  5. Mission 5When faiths met across oceans after 1492, why did some spread, some get banned and some grow new forms?
  6. Mission 6After 1750, did religion prop up power or help people challenge it?

Mission 1

Mission 1: Between 1200 and 1450, religions crossed oceans and deserts. Who actually carried them?

Make a guess: Between 1200 and 1450, religions crossed oceans and deserts. Who actually carried them?

Mission 1

Four carriers of belief

  • Between c. 1200 and c. 1450, trade networks (Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, trans-Saharan) grew busier.
  • Beliefs traveled with the people on them. Four main carriers:
  • Conquest: armies set up new rulers, who brought their faith and its institutions.
  • Merchants: traders settled in foreign ports, married locally, built places of worship.
  • Missionaries and Sufis: teachers and holy men who set out to share their faith.
  • Rulers' choices: a king adopts a faith, and his court and officials often follow.
  • Usually several carriers worked together, over generations.
Mission 1

Islam: conquest first, then merchants and Sufis

  • As the Abbasid Caliphate fragmented, Turkic Muslim rulers built new states.
  • Delhi Sultanate (from 1206): Turkic rulers conquered much of north India.
  • Conquest brought Muslim rule; it did not convert most people. Most South Asians stayed Hindu.
  • Conversion came more slowly through Sufis: mystics who sought closeness to God through love, poetry and music.
  • Sufi orders such as the Chishti (Mu'in al-Din Chishti, died 1236, at Ajmer) welcomed people of every caste; their shrines drew Hindu and Muslim visitors alike.
  • Merchants carried Islam further, by sea, to East Africa and Southeast Asia.
Quick check
?Which statement best describes how Islam spread in South Asia between c. 1200 and c. 1450?
Mission 1

Merchant diasporas

  • Diaspora: a community living away from its homeland. Merchant diasporas settled at key ports.
  • Swahili Coast (Kilwa, Mombasa, Mogadishu): Arab and Persian merchants married into Bantu-speaking communities. Islam spread; Swahili is a Bantu language with many Arabic words.
  • Malacca (founded c. 1400): its rulers became Muslim in the early 1400s, and the port helped carry Islam through the Malay world.
  • Chinese merchants settled in Southeast Asian ports; Admiral Zheng He, himself a Muslim, led Ming fleets there (1405–1433).
  • Malay sailors and traders formed communities around the Indian Ocean basin.
  • Influence ran both ways: merchants brought their faith, and local food, language, dress and customs changed the merchants.
Mission 1

Islam in West Africa

  • Muslim merchants crossed the Sahara with salt, gold and books.
  • West African rulers often adopted Islam first: it linked them to traders, literate officials and the wider Muslim world.
  • Mali: Muslim rulers; Timbuktu became a center of Islamic scholarship and manuscripts.
  • Many rulers also kept their traditional religious roles, and most farmers kept local beliefs for generations.
  • So Islam in West Africa spread from the top down and the city outward, mostly without conquest.
Quick check
?Which conclusion is best supported by the history of the Swahili Coast c. 1200–1450?
Mission 1

Chinese traditions and Buddhism in East Asia

  • Filial piety: duty and respect to parents and ancestors, a core Confucian value.
  • Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi, 1130–1200) joined Confucian ethics with ideas about the universe, partly in answer to Buddhism and Daoism.
  • It spread to Korea (Joseon dynasty from 1392 made it state orthodoxy), Vietnam (Confucian exams) and Japan (studied by Zen monks).
  • Buddhism kept shaping East Asia: Zen in Japan, Pure Land devotion, Tibetan Buddhism favored by the Mongol (Yuan) court.
  • Spread here came mostly through scholars, monks, books and diplomacy, not conquest.
Mission 1

Hindu and Buddhist states in South and Southeast Asia

  • Hinduism and Buddhism had reached Southeast Asia earlier, with Indian traders and Brahmin and Buddhist teachers.
  • Rulers adopted them to give kingship a sacred meaning.
  • Khmer Empire: Angkor Wat (12th century), built for Vishnu, later used for Buddhist worship.
  • Majapahit (Java, from 1293): a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom.
  • Theravada Buddhism, with monks trained in Sri Lanka, became the main faith in Burma, the Sukhothai kingdom (Thailand) and Cambodia during these centuries.
  • In South India, the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire rose in 1336.
Quick check
?A student says: "Hinduism and Buddhism spread to Southeast Asia mainly because Indian armies conquered the region." What is the best correction?
Mission 1

Travelers who wrote

  • Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69), a Muslim legal scholar from Morocco. Traveled about 30 years across Dar al-Islam: Mecca, East Africa, Delhi, the Maldives, China, Mali. His Rihla ("journey") was written down in 1355.
  • Margery Kempe (c. 1373–after 1438), an English Christian mystic from King's Lynn. Went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, Rome and Santiago de Compostela. The Book of Margery Kempe, dictated in the 1430s, is often called the first autobiography in English.
  • Marco Polo (1254–1324), a Venetian merchant, described the Mongol court of Kublai Khan.
  • Why more travelers: safer routes, busier trade, and pilgrimage (hajj for Muslims; holy places for Christians).
  • Their writings are evidence, but each writer judged what he or she saw from inside his or her own faith.
Mission 1Read the source

Ibn Battuta in Mali

Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352–53. In summary (Rihla, paraphrase):

  • He praised the people's care for prayer, crowds at Friday prayer, and their effort to learn the Qur'an by heart.
  • He praised the safety of the roads: travelers had no fear of robbers.
  • He disapproved that some women and servant girls went uncovered in public, and that people threw dust on their heads before the king.

Q1 What does his praise show about Islam in Mali?

Show answer

It was well established among many people, with mosques and Qur'an learning.

Q2 How does his point of view shape what he criticizes?

Show answer

As a scholar of Islamic law from North Africa, he judged local customs that differed from his own as wrong.

Mission 1

Why new and old practices lived together

  • New believers rarely dropped everything at once.
  • Rulers often converted first; villagers kept older customs for generations.
  • Teachers used local languages, music and stories. In Java, Muslim teachers later used shadow-puppet theater (wayang) to teach.
  • People added new practices alongside older ones: in Japan, many honored both Buddhas and local kami spirits.
  • Sufi shrines and Buddhist monasteries became shared local holy places.
  • Most believers saw their practice as their faith, expressed in their own culture, not as a mixture.
Mission 1Worked answer

Comparing two spreads

Question: Explain one difference between how Islam spread in South Asia and in West Africa, c. 1200–1450.

  • Point: in north India, Islam's spread followed military conquest; in West Africa, it arrived mainly with merchants.
  • Evidence: Turkic armies founded the Delhi Sultanate (1206); in Mali, rulers adopted Islam through contact with trans-Saharan traders.
  • Explanation: so in South Asia Muslim rule came before most conversion (which came later, via Sufis), while in West Africa rulers chose Islam for trade and learning links, and most farmers kept older beliefs.
  • AP tip: a comparison needs both sides and a word like "while" or "whereas."
Mission check

?In a 15th-century port of the Malay world, the ruler becomes Muslim after years of trade with Muslim merchants. Sufi teachers preach in the Malay language and use local stories. Many villagers keep honoring local spirits. Which pattern does this best fit?

Armies brought rulers; merchants, teachers and holy men usually brought believers, and local culture shaped what they brought.

Mission 2

Mission 2: How did a split inside Western Christianity end up spreading the faith around the world?

Make a guess: How did a split inside Western Christianity end up spreading the faith around the world?

Mission 2

Pressures for reform

  • By 1500 the Catholic Church led Western Christianity, with the pope at its head.
  • Critics attacked wealthy, worldly clergy and the sale of indulgences (release from some of the punishment still due for sins already forgiven; granted for prayers and good works, and by then often for money).
  • Renaissance humanists (e.g. Erasmus) urged a return to the Bible in its original languages.
  • The printing press (c. 1450s) spread new ideas fast and cheaply.
  • Earlier reformers, such as John Wycliffe (England) and Jan Hus (Bohemia), had been condemned.
Mission 2

Luther breaks with Rome

  • Martin Luther (1483–1546), a German monk and professor.
  • 1517: his Ninety-five Theses challenged the sale of indulgences.
  • Key ideas: salvation by faith alone (sola fide), the Bible alone as final authority (sola scriptura), the priesthood of all believers.
  • Kept two sacraments (baptism and the Lord's Supper) instead of seven.
  • Excommunicated (1521); protected by German princes; translated the New Testament into German (1522).
  • Peace of Augsburg (1555): each German ruler chose Lutheran or Catholic for his lands.
Mission 2Read the source

Faith and works

Translation: World English Bible, British Edition (WEBBE).

  • "But the righteous shall live by faith." (Romans 1:17)
  • "We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law." (Romans 3:28)
  • Catholic teaching also cites: "You see then that by works a man is justified, and not only by faith." (James 2:24)

Q1 Which verse supports Luther's sola fide?

Show answer

Romans 3:28: justified by faith apart from works of the law.

Q2 Why would Catholic theologians point to James 2:24?

Show answer

To show that faith and good works belong together in salvation.

Mission 2

Many Protestant churches

  • John Calvin (1509–1564), Geneva: God's sovereignty and predestination (God chooses who will be saved).
  • Calvin's Reformed churches spread to Switzerland, France (Huguenots), the Netherlands, Scotland (Presbyterians) and among English Puritans.
  • England: Henry VIII broke with the pope (Act of Supremacy, 1534), mainly for political and marriage reasons; the Church of England later took Protestant forms.
  • Anabaptists baptized only adult believers; persecuted by Catholics and other Protestants.
  • Protestantism became many churches, not one.
Quick check
?Which belief was central to Luther's break with the Catholic Church?
Mission 2

The Catholic Reformation

  • The Catholic Church reformed itself and answered Protestant ideas (also called the Counter-Reformation).
  • Council of Trent (1545–1563):
  • Reaffirmed seven sacraments, the authority of Scripture and Tradition, and salvation by God's grace received through faith with good works.
  • Banned abuses such as selling indulgences; required seminaries to train priests; bishops to live in their dioceses.
  • New religious orders and a confident style of art and architecture (Baroque).
Mission 2

Jesuits and global missions

  • Society of Jesus (Jesuits): founded by Ignatius of Loyola, approved 1540.
  • Schools and universities across Europe; won back regions such as Poland and southern Germany.
  • Francis Xavier (1506–1552): missions in India and Japan (1549).
  • Matteo Ricci (1552–1610) in Ming China learned Chinese and adapted to Confucian scholar culture.
  • With Franciscans and Dominicans, Jesuits worked in the Americas, the Philippines and Africa.
Mission 2Diversity

Three Christian traditions by 1600

  • Catholic: pope as head; seven sacraments; Scripture and Tradition; Mass in Latin; saints, Mary and monasteries central.
  • Orthodox: patriarchs and church councils; seven sacraments (mysteries); icons; liturgy in Greek, Slavonic and other languages.
  • Protestant: no pope; Bible as final authority; usually two sacraments; services in local languages; married clergy; many separate churches.
  • All share belief in the Trinity, the incarnation and the resurrection.
Quick check
?Which was a decision of the Council of Trent?
Mission 2

Religion, rivalry and empire

  • Catholic Spain and Portugal led early maritime empires; the pope backed their division of new lands (Treaty of Tordesillas, 1494).
  • Kings saw spreading Catholic Christianity as a duty and a justification for conquest.
  • Protestant England and the Dutch Republic challenged Spain for religious as well as political and economic reasons (e.g. the Spanish Armada, 1588; the Dutch revolt against Spain).
  • Missions followed empire: Catholic orders baptized millions in the Americas and the Philippines; the Kongo kingdom's rulers became Catholic.
  • Both reformations grew Christianity: Protestant churches multiplied in Europe and its colonies; Catholic missions made it a world religion.
Mission 2

Religion and abolition

  • 1700s–1800s: Enlightenment ideas of natural rights met religious ideals.
  • Quakers taught "that of God in every one"; Germantown Quakers protested slavery (1688), and Quakers were most of the founders of Britain's abolition society (1787).
  • Evangelical Christians such as William Wilberforce campaigned in Parliament; Olaudah Equiano, a formerly enslaved writer, used Christian arguments.
  • "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man… you are all one in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 3:28)
  • But many enslavers and churches also defended slavery using the Bible.
  • Britain ended its slave trade (1807) and slavery in most of its empire (1833).
Mission 2

Liberation theology

  • Latin America, 1960s–1980s: deep poverty and military dictatorships.
  • Liberation theology: God takes the side of the poor; faith must work to change unjust structures.
  • Gustavo Gutiérrez (1928–2024), Peru, A Theology of Liberation (1971); Latin American bishops at Medellín (1968) called the Church to stand with the poor; at Puebla (1979) they named a preferential option for the poor.
  • Key text: "he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor" (Luke 4:18)
  • Archbishop Óscar Romero of El Salvador spoke for the poor and was killed in 1980 (declared a saint, 2018).
  • The Vatican (1984) criticized its use of Marxist analysis while affirming concern for the poor.
Quick check
?How did liberation theology challenge older assumptions about religion in Latin America?
Mission check

?In the early 1500s, King Afonso I of Kongo, a Catholic, wrote to the king of Portugal asking for priests and teachers, while protesting against Portuguese slave traders. What does his case show?

The Reformation split Western Christianity, yet rival churches, empires and missions made it a global faith that later fueled reform movements.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Emperors, sultans and kings all claimed heaven was on their side. How did they make people believe it?

Make a guess: Emperors, sultans and kings all claimed heaven was on their side. How did they make people believe it?

Mission 3

Why rulers needed religion

  • Legitimacy: the belief, among subjects and elites, that a ruler has the right to rule.
  • Force alone is costly. Rulers who seemed chosen by God, the gods or Heaven needed less of it.
  • Four tools, used by almost every state, c. 1200–1750:
  • Religious ideas: the ruler is chosen, protected or descended from the divine.
  • Ritual: the ruler leads ceremonies, sacrifices or prayers.
  • Monuments and art: temples, mosques, tombs, palaces and portraits that display sacred power.
  • Religious officials: scholars, priests or monks who serve and support the state.
Mission 3

Song China: Confucian rule

  • Song dynasty (960–1279) justified its rule by Confucian ideas.
  • Mandate of Heaven: Heaven grants the right to rule to a just emperor and withdraws it from an unjust one.
  • An imperial bureaucracy of scholar-officials, chosen by civil service exams on the Confucian classics, ran the empire.
  • Confucian values of order, filial piety and loyalty made obedience to the emperor a moral duty.
  • Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi) strengthened this link between moral order and political order.
Mission 3

Caliphs and sultans

  • Caliph ("successor" to the Prophet Muhammad): leader of the Muslim community, a religious and political title.
  • The Abbasid Caliphate fragmented; real power passed to new, mostly Turkic states.
  • Sultan ("authority"): a ruler with military and political power, often recognized by the caliph. The Seljuk Turks received the title in Baghdad in 1055.
  • The Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258. The Mamluk sultans of Egypt kept an Abbasid caliph in Cairo as a symbol of their legitimacy.
  • Sultans won support by enforcing sharia, funding mosques and madrasas, and protecting pilgrims; e.g. the Delhi Sultanate (1206).
Mission 3

Hindu and Buddhist kingship

  • New Hindu and Buddhist states arose in South and Southeast Asia: Vijayanagara (1336), the Khmer Empire, Majapahit, the Sukhothai kingdom, Rajput kingdoms.
  • Hindu kings presented themselves as protectors of dharma (sacred order and duty) and built great temples to their chosen deity.
  • Buddhist kings in Theravada lands presented themselves as dhamma-kings who protected and funded the sangha (community of monks).
  • The temple or monastery was a center of worship, learning, land and wealth: supporting it showed a king's merit.
  • Angkor Wat joined royal power with Vishnu, the cosmos and later the Buddha.
Quick check
?Which comparison of state legitimacy, c. 1200–1450, is accurate?
Mission 3

Mexica and Inca state religion

  • Mexica (Aztec): teaching held that the gods had given their own blood to set the sun moving. Humans owed a debt in return.
  • Offerings of blood, including the sacrifice of war captives, were believed to nourish the sun and keep the world from ending.
  • The ruler led these rites at the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan, shrine of Huitzilopochtli (sun and war) and Tlaloc (rain). Religion joined warfare, tribute and kingship.
  • Inca: the ruler (Sapa Inca) was honored as the son of Inti, the sun.
  • The Coricancha ("golden enclosure"), the sun temple in Cuzco, sat at the sacred center of the empire. Past rulers' mummies were kept and honored as living presences.
Mission 3

Christian Ethiopia and Muslim Hausa rulers

  • Ethiopia: an ancient Christian kingdom. From 1270, the Solomonic dynasty claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.
  • The Kebra Nagast ("Glory of the Kings", 14th century) told this story and the Ark of the Covenant's journey to Ethiopia, making the kings sacred guardians.
  • Earlier rulers carved the rock-cut churches of Lalibela, built as a "new Jerusalem."
  • Hausa kingdoms (northern Nigeria): rulers adopted Islam through trade; Muhammad Rumfa of Kano (ruled 1463–99) promoted Islamic law and scholarship.
  • Many Hausa farmers kept older beliefs alongside Islam for centuries.
Mission 3

Divine right, Songhai and monuments, 1450–1750

  • Divine right (Europe): kings are appointed by God and answer to God alone, not to subjects; James VI of Scotland, later James I of England (The True Law of Free Monarchies, 1598), Louis XIV of France.
  • Songhai: Askia Muhammad (ruled 1493–1528) promoted Islam, went on hajj (1496–97), and was named the caliph's deputy in West Africa.
  • Mughal mausolea and mosques: the Taj Mahal (1632–53) and Lahore's Badshahi Mosque (1670s) proclaimed the emperor a pious Muslim ruler.
  • Inca sun temple of Cuzco; Versailles (Louis XIV); Qing imperial portraits.
  • Same pattern as before 1450, on a larger scale.
Quick check
?Which example best shows a ruler using monumental architecture to legitimize rule, 1450–1750?
Mission 3

Faith and rivalry between states

  • Ottoman vs Safavid: the Safavid Shah Ismail I made Twelver Shi'a Islam the state faith of Iran (1501). The Ottomans championed Sunni Islam.
  • They fought for land and power (Chaldiran, 1514), and each persecuted the other's supporters at home.
  • Their rivalry intensified the split between Sunni and Shi'a.
  • Safavid vs Mughal: fought over Kandahar; mostly a territorial rivalry, though one was Shi'a and the other Sunni.
  • Songhai vs Morocco: a Moroccan army defeated Songhai in 1591: both Muslim; the rivalry was over gold and trade.
  • Europe: wars between Catholic and Protestant states, including the Thirty Years' War (1618–48).
  • Religion could deepen rivalries, but it was rarely the only cause.
Mission 3

Accommodate or suppress?

  • Ottoman Empire: Christians and Jews were dhimmis (protected peoples), paid the jizya tax, and ran many of their own affairs under their own religious leaders (later called millets).
  • The Ottomans also took Christian boys by a levy (devshirme), converted them to Islam and trained them as soldiers (janissaries) and officials.
  • In 1492 Sultan Bayezid II welcomed Jews expelled from Spain.
  • Mughal Empire: Akbar abolished the jizya (1564), employed Hindu Rajput nobles and hosted debates among faiths (see Mission 5). Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya (1679).
  • Spain: the Alhambra Decree (1492) ordered Jews to convert or leave; Portugal followed (1496–97). Muslims were forced to convert; their descendants (Moriscos) were expelled in 1609–14.
  • Rulers chose accommodation to use subjects' skills, taxes and loyalty; others chose suppression to build religious unity.
Quick check
?A historian argues: "The Ottoman Empire accommodated religious diversity more than Spain did, 1450–1750." Which evidence best supports this?
Mission 3Worked answer

Comparing legitimacy

Question: Compare how two states used religion to legitimize rule, c. 1200–1750.

  • Similarity: both the Inca and the Mughals linked the ruler to the sacred and built monuments to show it: the Coricancha in Cuzco; the Taj Mahal and great mosques.
  • Difference: the Sapa Inca was honored as son of the sun, a divine descent; Mughal emperors, as Muslims, claimed no divinity but presented themselves as just, pious rulers.
  • Explanation: each used the religious ideas its subjects already held, so obedience to the ruler felt like obedience to the sacred order.
  • AP tip: name both states in every sentence of a comparison.
Mission check

?In 1547, Ivan IV of Moscow was crowned "tsar" by the head of the Russian Orthodox Church. Churchmen called Moscow the "Third Rome," heir of Christian Rome and Constantinople. He then built St. Basil's Cathedral to celebrate a victory. What do these actions best illustrate?

Across very different faiths, rulers did the same things: claimed sacred approval, led rituals, built monuments and chose whom to tolerate.

Mission 4

Mission 4: Guru Nanak grew up among Hindus and Muslims. Why do Sikhs say their faith is neither?

Make a guess: Guru Nanak grew up among Hindus and Muslims. Why do Sikhs say their faith is neither?

Mission 4

Punjab around 1500

  • Punjab: the "land of five rivers," in today's northern India and Pakistan.
  • Ruled by Muslim sultans (the Lodi dynasty of Delhi); conquered by Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, in 1526.
  • Most villagers were Hindus; rulers, many officials and a growing number of villagers were Muslims.
  • Two devotional movements crossed the line between them:
  • Bhakti (Hindu): loving devotion to God, open to every caste, sung in local languages.
  • Sufism (Muslim): seeking closeness to God through love, music and poetry.
  • Poet-saints such as Kabir (15th century) mocked empty ritual on both sides.
Mission 4

Guru Nanak

  • Guru Nanak (1469–1539), born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan) to a Hindu family; worked for a Muslim official at Sultanpur.
  • Sikh tradition: around 1499 he disappeared into a river for three days and returned with a message from God.
  • His first words, as the janamsakhis (traditional life stories) remember them: "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim."
  • Most Sikhs read this as: God sees people, not religious labels; all are equal before God.
  • He traveled widely, then founded a farming community at Kartarpur, where his followers worked, prayed and ate together.
  • Sikh means "learner" or "disciple." Guru is often explained as a teacher who leads from darkness to light.
Mission 4

One God, the Name and the Guru

  • Sikhism is monotheistic. The scripture opens with Ik Onkar: "There is one God."
  • The opening verse (the Mool Mantar) describes God as true, the Creator, without fear or hatred, timeless, never born, known through the Guru's grace (Guru Granth Sahib 1, paraphrase).
  • Sikhs often call God Waheguru ("Wonderful Lord").
  • Sikhs believe God is beyond form and never takes human birth: no idols, no incarnations.
  • The goal: freedom from rebirth through remembering God's Name (nam simran), honest work and sharing.
  • Links to the setting, and a break from it: rebirth and karma are shared with Hindu thought; one formless God sounds close to Islam; but Sikhs regard the message as a fresh revelation from God to Nanak.
Mission 4

Equality in practice

  • Guru Nanak rejected caste rank, idol worship, pilgrimage as a path to God, and the separation of women.
  • Langar: a free kitchen where everyone sits on the floor in rows and eats the same food, whatever their caste, religion or wealth.
  • Seva: selfless service to others (cooking in the langar, cleaning, helping strangers).
  • Gurdwara ("door of the Guru"): the Sikh place of worship, open to all. Every gurdwara has a langar; the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar has four doors as a sign of this welcome.
  • Sikh tradition: the Mughal emperor Akbar sat on the floor and ate in the langar before meeting the third Guru, Amar Das.
  • In a caste society, eating together was a public, daily rejection of rank.
Quick check
?A historian wants to show that early Sikhism challenged the social order of 16th-century Punjab. Which practice is the strongest evidence?
Mission 4

A scripture with many voices

  • The fifth Guru, Arjan, compiled the Adi Granth (1604) and placed it in the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), Amritsar.
  • It held hymns by the first five Gurus, written in the Gurmukhi script; Guru Gobind Singh later added those of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur (six Gurus in all).
  • It also holds hymns by bhagats ("devotees") from other communities: Ravidas and Namdev from Hindu backgrounds, Kabir, a weaver from a Muslim family who rejected both labels, and the Muslim Sufi Sheikh Farid.
  • Sikhs include them because their words agree with the Gurus' teaching about one God and equality, not because Sikhism is a mixture.
  • Historians use this as evidence of the context of interactions in which Sikhism grew.
Mission 4

Ten Gurus and the Mughal emperors

  • After Nanak came nine more human Gurus, ending with Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708).
  • Akbar (ruled 1556–1605) tolerated and respected the Gurus.
  • Guru Arjan was executed in Lahore in 1606, under Emperor Jahangir. Sikhs honor him as the first Sikh martyr.
  • His son Guru Hargobind wore two swords: miri (worldly power) and piri (spiritual authority). Sikhs began to defend themselves.
  • Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed in Delhi in 1675, under Aurangzeb. Sikh tradition says he gave his life defending the right of Hindus (Kashmiri Pandits) to practice their own faith.
  • Relations depended on the emperor's policy, not simply on "Hindu versus Muslim."
Mission 4

The Khalsa, 1699

  • Sikh tradition tells that at the spring festival of Vaisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked who would give their head for their faith.
  • Five men from different castes and regions stepped forward: the Panj Pyare ("five beloved ones").
  • He initiated them with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a sword), and they initiated him: the Khalsa ("the pure") was born.
  • Khalsa men take the name Singh ("lion"), women Kaur ("princess"); caste names are dropped.
  • Khalsa Sikhs keep the Five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kangha (comb), kara (steel bracelet), kachera (cotton undergarment), kirpan (sword).
  • Before his death in 1708, Guru Gobind Singh ended the line of human Gurus: the scripture became the Guru Granth Sahib, the living Guru.
Mission 4Read the source

"Neither Hindu nor Muslim"

A hymn by Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib says, in summary (Guru Granth Sahib 1136, paraphrase):

  • I do not keep the Hindu fasts or the Muslim fast of Ramadan.
  • I do not go on pilgrimage to Hindu holy places or to Mecca.
  • I serve only the One God, who is both Allah and Ram.
  • I am neither Hindu nor Muslim: my body and breath belong to the One.

Q1 What evidence in the hymn shows the Hindu and Muslim setting?

Show answer

It names their practices and their names for God.

Q2 How does the hymn mark Sikh identity as distinct?

Show answer

It sets aside both sets of rituals and serves the One God directly.

Mission 4Diversity

Who counts as a Sikh?

  • Amritdhari: Sikhs who have taken amrit and joined the Khalsa; they keep the Five Ks and the Khalsa code of conduct.
  • Keshdhari: Sikhs who keep uncut hair (and often a turban) but have not taken amrit.
  • Sahajdhari: Sikhs who follow the Gurus' teachings but have not taken amrit and may cut their hair; the word is often explained as "gradual adopters."
  • Most Sikh institutions see the Khalsa as the ideal, and many sahajdharis as Sikhs on the way to it.
  • How far sahajdharis count as full Sikhs (for example, in voting for gurdwara committees) is debated among Sikhs today.
Quick check
?Harpreet prays daily, reads from the Guru Granth Sahib and serves in the langar. He trims his beard and has not taken amrit. Which term do Sikhs most often use for him?
Mission 4Evaluate

How far did its Hindu and Muslim setting shape early Sikhism?

  • Shaped a lot: Punjabi language and poetry; shared ideas of karma and rebirth; names for God from both traditions (Ram, Hari, Allah); bhagat hymns in the scripture; a style close to bhakti and Sufi devotion.
  • Distinct from both: rejects both sets of rituals and labels (Guru Granth Sahib 1136); new institutions (a line of Gurus, its own scripture and script, langar, the Khalsa); most Sikhs regard it as a revelation from God, not a combination of older faiths.
  • Historians' debate: older Western writers often called Sikhism a "syncretism" (a blend). Most scholars now avoid that word; some still stress its links with the Sant (poet-saint) tradition.
  • Judge it by: Do shared words mean shared beliefs? Whose view counts as evidence: insiders or outsiders? What was new that neither tradition had?
Mission 4Worked answer

Explaining context

Question: Explain one way in which Sikhism developed in a context of interactions between Hinduism and Islam.

  • Claim: Sikhism grew in Mughal Punjab, where Hindu and Muslim communities and devotional movements met.
  • Evidence: the Guru Granth Sahib includes hymns by bhagats from Hindu backgrounds such as Ravidas and Namdev and by the Muslim Sufi Sheikh Farid.
  • Explanation: the Gurus accepted voices from both communities whose teaching matched their own (one God, equality), while rejecting both communities' rituals and caste rank, creating a distinct faith.
  • AP tip: an "explain" answer needs the how or why (the because), not just a fact.
Mission check

?A museum label reads: "Sikhism: a blend of Hinduism and Islam." Which rewrite is most accurate, both to the AP framework and to how most Sikhs understand their faith?

Context is not the same as content. Sikhism grew where Hindus and Muslims met, and Sikhs see it as its own revelation.

Mission 5

Mission 5: When faiths met across oceans after 1492, why did some spread, some get banned and some grow new forms?

Make a guess: When faiths met across oceans after 1492, why did some spread, some get banned and some grow new forms?

Mission 5

Faith as a motive for empire

  • European maritime empires (Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, French, British) grew from political, religious and economic rivalries.
  • 1492: Castile and Aragon complete the Reconquista, the Christian conquest of Muslim Granada, and Columbus sails west.
  • Popes granted Portugal and Spain the right to claim new lands and the duty to convert their peoples; the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the claims between them.
  • After the Reformation, Protestant Dutch and English challenged Catholic Spain and Portugal at sea: rivalry over trade and over faith.
  • The wish to spread Christianity sat alongside gold, land and glory; historians debate how much each mattered.
  • Later, 1750–1900, the wish to convert Indigenous peoples was again used to justify empire (see Mission 6).
Mission 5

Missions on three continents

  • Catholic religious orders led missions: Franciscans, Dominicans and the new Jesuits (founded 1540).
  • Americas: twelve Franciscans reached Mexico in 1524; missionaries learned Nahuatl and other languages, baptized millions (by their own count), and destroyed temples and images of the old gods.
  • Africa: the king of Kongo was baptized in 1491; his son Afonso I (ruled 1509–1542) made Catholicism the faith of the court, by choice.
  • Asia: Francis Xavier reached Japan in 1549; Matteo Ricci (in China from 1582) dressed as a Confucian scholar and presented Christianity in Confucian terms.
  • Methods ranged from persuasion and adapting to local culture to conversion under colonial force.
Quick check
?Which pairing correctly matches a region with how Catholic Christianity mainly arrived there, c. 1450–1750?
Mission 5

Conversion meets resistance

  • Japan: at the peak, around 1600, perhaps 300,000 Christians. Rulers feared divided loyalties and foreign power.
  • Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered missionaries out (1587); the Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity (1614).
  • After the Shimabara Rebellion (1637–38), Japan limited European trade to the Dutch at Nagasaki; hidden Christians (Kakure Kirishitan) kept their faith in secret for over 200 years.
  • China: emperors tolerated Jesuit scholars but later restricted Christian preaching after the pope rejected Chinese rites honoring ancestors and Confucius.
  • New Mexico: in the Pueblo Revolt (1680), Pueblo peoples drove out the Spanish, partly because Franciscans had suppressed their ceremonies.
  • Contact caused religious conflict as well as conversion.
Mission 5Read the source

A Confucian adviser questions a missionary

In 1709, Arai Hakuseki (1657–1725), adviser to the Tokugawa shogun, questioned Giovanni Battista Sidotti, an Italian priest who had entered Japan in defiance of the ban. In summary (paraphrase of Arai's report):

  • Christians say all love and reverence belong to God, the Creator and Lord.
  • Then a person would hold back love from his real father and reverence from his real lord. Arai calls this disloyal and impious.
  • Worshipping the Lord of Heaven is the emperor's duty, not ordinary people's: the sovereign is Heaven to subjects, as a father is Heaven to his child.

Q1 Which long-standing tradition shapes Arai's argument?

Show answer

Confucianism: filial piety and loyalty to the ruler.

Q2 Why might a government see Christianity as a political threat, not just a religious one?

Show answer

It seemed to put loyalty to God, and to a foreign Church, above loyalty to ruler and father.

Mission 5

A different answer: Akbar

  • Not every ruler banned or imposed a faith.
  • The Mughal emperor Akbar (ruled 1556–1605) governed a Hindu majority as a Muslim ruler.
  • He abolished the jizya (tax on non-Muslims) in 1564.
  • In his House of Worship (Ibadat Khana, 1575) at Fatehpur Sikri, he hosted debates among Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and, from 1580, Jesuit scholars.
  • His policy was called sulh-i kul, "peace with all."
  • So responses to religious encounter ranged from bans (Japan) to tolerance and debate (Akbar) to new traditions (next screens).
Quick check
?Which statement correctly describes the Tokugawa response to Christianity?
Mission 5

What "syncretic" means

  • Syncretic: a belief system or practice shaped by more than one religious tradition, through contact.
  • In the Atlantic world, African, American and European peoples all contributed to a new cultural synthesis (in food, music, language and religion).
  • For enslaved Africans and conquered Indigenous peoples, holding on to older beliefs inside Christian forms could be a way to survive and resist.
  • Careful: many practitioners reject the idea that their faith is a "mixture." To them it is a complete religion in its own right.
  • Historians use "syncretic" for how a tradition formed, not as a judgment that it is less authentic.
Mission 5

The Virgin of Guadalupe

  • Catholic tradition: in December 1531, the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego, a Nahua (Aztec) convert, on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City. She spoke to him in Nahuatl.
  • Her image, believed by Catholics to be miraculously imprinted on his cloak, is honored in the Basilica of Guadalupe.
  • Historians note that Tepeyac had been a sacred site for a Nahua mother goddess, and that the image uses symbols Nahua people would recognize.
  • The Catholic Church regards Guadalupe as fully Catholic devotion to Mary, not a blend; Juan Diego was declared a saint in 2002.
  • Guadalupe became a symbol of Mexican identity, uniting Indigenous, mestizo and Spanish Mexicans.
Mission 5

Vodou and Santería

  • Enslaved Africans brought their religions across the Atlantic, especially from West and Central Africa (Yoruba, Fon, Kongo peoples).
  • Colonial law required baptism; Africans kept serving their spirits, often linked to Catholic saints.
  • Vodou (Haiti): one distant creator God (Bondye); spirits called lwa are served with drumming, song and offerings. Danbala, a serpent spirit, is linked with St. Patrick.
  • Santería (Cuba), also called Regla de Ocha or Lucumí: Yoruba spirits called orishas. Changó is linked with St. Barbara; Ochún with Our Lady of Charity.
  • Both took shape over the 1600s–1800s and are living religions today, in the Caribbean and the United States.
Quick check
?Which statement about Vodou and Santería would most practitioners and historians accept?
Mission 5

Everyone contributed

  • Kongo: Catholicism took Kongo forms; Kikongo words for God and spirits were used in Christian teaching.
  • Kimpa Vita (Dona Beatriz), a young Kongolese woman, taught (1704–06) that St. Anthony spoke through her and that Jesus had been born in Kongo. She was burned as a heretic in 1706; her movement drew thousands.
  • Some Kongolese Catholics were carried to the Americas as enslaved people, bringing Christian and Kongo beliefs together.
  • Europeans changed too: Atlantic food (maize, potatoes, chocolate), music and words.
  • The framework's point: in the Atlantic world, all parties contributed to cultural synthesis, even under deep inequality.
Mission 5Evaluate

"Between 1450 and 1750, contact spread religions mainly through force."

  • Reasons for: conquest of the Americas; temples and images destroyed; colonial law required baptism of enslaved Africans; Spain's Inquisition; forced baptism of Jews and Muslims in Spain and Portugal.
  • Reasons against: Kongo's kings chose Catholicism; Jesuits in China and Japan relied on persuasion; Akbar's court debated freely; Nahua converts made Guadalupe their own; Vodou and Santería show enslaved people shaping their own faith.
  • Judge it by: Which regions? (Americas vs Asia vs Africa.) Whose sources: missionaries, rulers or converts? What counts as "force": armies, laws, or pressure from inequality?
Mission check

?In Bahia, Brazil, followers of Candomblé honor Yoruba spirits called orixás with drumming and dance; some temples also join in Catholic festivals of the saints. The tradition grew among enslaved Africans in the 1700s–1800s. Which development of 1450–1750 does this best illustrate?

Contact did three things at once: it spread religions, caused conflict, and gave rise to new traditions that their followers regard as fully their own.

Mission 6

Mission 6: After 1750, did religion prop up power or help people challenge it?

Make a guess: After 1750, did religion prop up power or help people challenge it?

Mission 6

The Enlightenment and religion in public life

  • The Enlightenment (c. 1680–1800) stressed reason, evidence and natural rights, and questioned traditions, including the power of established churches.
  • John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689): the state should protect life, liberty and property, not force belief.
  • Deists believed in a Creator known by reason, not through miracles or churches; others, such as Voltaire, attacked church power.
  • Many Enlightenment thinkers were believers who wanted toleration, not the end of religion.
  • U.S. First Amendment (1791): "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."
  • The French Revolution went further: it seized Church lands (1789) and put clergy under state control (1790).
Mission 6

Faith and reason against slavery

  • Reform movements drew on both Enlightenment natural rights and religious ideals.
  • Quakers (Society of Friends) believed there is "that of God" in every person; Philadelphia Quakers barred slaveholders from membership in 1776.
  • Evangelical Christians such as William Wilberforce campaigned in Parliament; Black Christians such as Olaudah Equiano (1789 memoir) and Frederick Douglass wrote and spoke against slavery.
  • Results: Britain ended its slave trade (1807) and slavery in its empire (1833); the U.S. abolished slavery (1865); Brazil (1888). Russia ended serfdom (1861).
  • Defenders of slavery also cited the Bible (e.g. Ephesians 6:5): religion was used on both sides.
Mission 6Read the source

"One blood"

"He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth" (Acts 17:26)

  • Abolitionists often quoted this verse (in the King James wording, "of one blood all nations of men").
  • The British anti-slavery medallion of 1787 showed a kneeling, chained man with the words: "Am I not a man and a brother?"

Q1 Which religious idea did abolitionists draw from this verse?

Show answer

All peoples share one origin from God, so all are equally human.

Q2 How does the medallion's question join a religious ideal to an Enlightenment idea?

Show answer

"Brother" appeals to Christian fellowship; "man" appeals to shared human nature and natural rights.

Quick check
?Which statement best describes the role of religion in the abolition of slavery, 1750–1900?
Mission 6

Religion and new nations

  • Nationalism: loyalty to a nation, a people who share language, customs, territory and often religion.
  • Balkan nationalisms: Orthodox Christian Greeks (independent 1830) and Serbs built national identities against Muslim Ottoman rule.
  • Ottomanism: Ottoman reformers (Tanzimat, 1839–76) tried the opposite, making Muslims, Christians and Jews equal Ottoman citizens.
  • Governments sometimes used a shared faith to foster unity; minority faiths could then be treated as outsiders.
  • Religion could unite a nation or divide an empire.
Mission 6

Faith as a justification for empire

  • Imperialists, 1750–1900, justified rule with Social Darwinism, nationalism, the civilizing mission, and the desire to convert Indigenous peoples.
  • Missionaries traveled with, or ahead of, empire: David Livingstone called for "Christianity, commerce and civilization" in Africa (paraphrase of his 1857 lectures).
  • Mission schools and hospitals spread literacy and medicine, and also European languages and values.
  • Some missionaries protested colonial abuses; e.g. missionaries in the Congo photographed and publicized atrocities.
  • Many Africans and Asians made Christianity their own, founding independent churches led by local Christians.
Mission 6

Rebellions shaped by religion

  • Xhosa Cattle-Killing (southern Africa, 1856–57): the young prophet Nongqawuse said the ancestors would return and drive out the British if people killed their cattle; famine followed.
  • Sokoto Caliphate (West Africa, from 1804): Usman dan Fodio led a jihad against Hausa rulers he judged unjust, creating a new Islamic state.
  • Mahdist wars (Sudan, 1881–98): Muhammad Ahmad, proclaimed the Mahdi (a redeemer awaited in Muslim tradition), drove out Egyptian and British forces and took Khartoum (1885).
  • Ghost Dance (U.S., 1889–90): the Paiute prophet Wovoka taught a dance that would renew the world and reunite the living with their dead. Fear of it led to the massacre at Wounded Knee (1890).
  • In each, religious hope gave people a reason to resist when other means had failed.
Quick check
?What do the Ghost Dance, the Mahdist movement and the Xhosa Cattle-Killing have in common?
Mission 6

Religion against colonial boundaries

  • After 1900, regional, religious and ethnic movements challenged colonial rule and the borders empires had drawn.
  • Muslim League (founded 1906) in British India: argued that India's Muslims were a nation with their own interests.
  • The Lahore Resolution (1940) called for independent Muslim-majority states.
  • In 1947 British India was partitioned into India and Pakistan; huge migrations and violence followed.
  • Other movements were mainly regional or ethnic (Québécois separatism in Canada; the Biafra secession in Nigeria): religion was one marker of identity among several.
Mission 6

Nonviolence

  • Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948): satyagraha ("truth-force"), nonviolent mass resistance to British rule, e.g. the Salt March (1930). Drew on Hindu and Jain ahimsa (non-harm), the Bhagavad Gita, Jesus' Sermon on the Mount and Tolstoy.
  • Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968): a Baptist minister who joined Christian love of enemies with Gandhi's methods in the U.S. civil rights movement (Montgomery bus boycott, 1955–56).
  • Nelson Mandela (1918–2013): helped lead the ANC's nonviolent Defiance Campaign (1952) as its volunteer-in-chief; after the Sharpeville massacre (1960) he helped found an armed wing (1961); after prison (1962–90) he led a negotiated, peaceful transition to democracy (president 1994).
  • Religion shaped Gandhi's and King's nonviolence directly; Mandela's reasons were more political and moral.
Mission 6

Rights, liberation theology and inclusion

  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), Article 18: "Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion."
  • Liberation theology (Latin America, from the late 1960s): Catholic theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez (1928–2024; A Theology of Liberation, 1971) taught that God takes the side of the poor and that faith calls Christians to change unjust structures.
  • Latin American bishops spoke of a "preferential option for the poor." Archbishop Óscar Romero was killed in El Salvador (1980) after speaking out for the poor; the Catholic Church declared him a saint in 2018.
  • The Vatican (1984) criticized the use of Marxist ideas in some liberation theology, while keeping concern for the poor.
  • Inclusion: India's constitution (1950) banned discrimination by religion; the Catholic Church affirmed religious freedom (1965).
  • Inclusion in roles: religious tests for office and universities were dropped. In Britain, Catholics could sit in Parliament from 1829 and Jews from 1858; Oxford and Cambridge opened degrees to non-Anglicans in 1871.
Quick check
?Which statement about the three leaders named in the AP framework is accurate?
Mission 6Evaluate

"After 1750, religion did more to challenge political power than to support it."

  • Reasons for: abolitionists; rebellions (Mahdi, Ghost Dance, Sokoto); Gandhi and King; liberation theology; churches that opposed apartheid and dictatorships.
  • Reasons against: religion justified imperialism (civilizing mission, converting Indigenous peoples); defenders of slavery cited scripture; national churches backed states; religious nationalism helped divide India in 1947.
  • Another view: "religion" is not one actor: the same faith served rulers and rebels, often at the same time.
  • Judge it by: Which region and decade? Who is using religion: governments, clergy, or ordinary believers? Does "support" include staying silent?
Mission check

?In the Philippines in 1986, Cardinal Jaime Sin called on Catholics to fill a Manila highway. Priests, nuns and crowds praying the rosary stood unarmed in front of army tanks. The dictator Ferdinand Marcos fled the country. Which development does this best illustrate?

After 1750, religion did both: it justified empires and inspired those who resisted them; which side it served depended on who was using it.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Islam spread by conquest (Delhi Sultanate), then by merchants, missionaries and Sufis; in West Africa and around the Indian Ocean mainly by trade.
  • Merchant diasporas (Swahili Coast, Malacca, Chinese and Malay communities) introduced traditions and were changed by local cultures; Neo-Confucianism and Buddhism shaped East Asia; Hindu and Buddhist states rose in South and Southeast Asia.
  • Travelers such as Ibn Battuta and Margery Kempe wrote about their journeys, judging what they saw from their own faith.

Mission 2

  • Luther (1517) and other Protestants broke with Rome over salvation, authority and sacraments; the Catholic Reformation (Trent, 1545–1563; Jesuits) answered.
  • Both reformations grew Christianity: missions followed rival empires to the Americas, Asia and Africa.
  • Religious ideals helped drive abolition and, in the 20th century, liberation theology; Christians stood on both sides of these debates.

Mission 3

  • Rulers used religious ideas, ritual, monuments and religious officials to legitimize power: Confucian bureaucracy and the Mandate of Heaven; caliphs and Turkic sultans; Hindu and Buddhist kings; Mexica and Inca state religion; Solomonic Ethiopia; Hausa and Songhai Islam; European divine right; Mughal mosques and tombs.
  • Religious and political disputes fed rivalries (Ottoman–Safavid, deepening the Sunni–Shi'a split), though rarely as the only cause.
  • Some states accommodated diversity (Ottomans, Akbar); others suppressed it (Spain's expulsion of Jews, 1492).

Mission 4

  • Guru Nanak (1469–1539) taught one God, equality and honest work in a Punjab shaped by Hindu bhakti, Muslim rule and Sufism.
  • Langar, seva, the gurdwara and a scripture with voices from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds show the context of interactions; Sikhs regard the faith as distinct, not a blend.
  • Mughal relations ranged from Akbar's respect to the executions of Guru Arjan (1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675); the Khalsa (1699) and the Guru Granth Sahib (1708) shaped Sikh identity, with amritdhari, keshdhari and sahajdhari Sikhs today.

Mission 5

  • Religious rivalry, alongside political and economic rivalry, drove European maritime empires; missions reached the Americas, Africa and Asia by persuasion and by force.
  • Responses varied: conversion (Kongo), bans and persecution (Tokugawa Japan), revolt (Pueblo), tolerance and debate (Akbar).
  • In the Atlantic world all peoples contributed to cultural synthesis; Guadalupe, Vodou and Santería grew from contact and are living traditions on their own terms.

Mission 6

  • The Enlightenment reexamined religion's role in public life (toleration, the First Amendment), while Enlightenment and religious ideals together drove abolition and other reforms.
  • Religion helped build nations, justify empire (the desire to convert), and inspire rebellions (Xhosa Cattle-Killing, Sokoto, Mahdist wars, Ghost Dance) and anti-colonial movements (Muslim League).
  • Gandhi, King and Mandela promoted nonviolence; rights-based discourses such as liberation theology and the UDHR challenged old assumptions and widened religious inclusion.
